_note: Buy-it-or-make-it comparisons. `store_query` finds the best store version; `ingredients` are the things you would buy instead, each with `uses` = the fraction of the purchased package one batch consumes, which is what makes a cost-per-batch estimate possible. Every term was checked against the real catalog (scripts/check_meals.py covers meals; these were checked the same way) - 'honey' matched Honeycrisp APPLES and 'baking powder' matched baking COCOA before being pinned down. Chosen by measuring the gap between the best store version and the average score of what you would buy: only items with a real gap are here. `yield_oz` is the approximate finished weight of one batch. Without it the cost line compared a batch against a package and implied homemade granola costs $11.40 against the store's $6.29 - but the batch makes about 21 oz and the bag is 11.5 oz, so per ounce they are nearly identical. A cost comparison with mismatched units is worse than none. Items with `no_good_option` were chosen by scanning every category for ones where even the BEST product scores badly - muffins top out at 9, biscuits at 13, honey mustard dressing at 28. There the app's normal job (find you the best one) has no useful answer, so the honest answer is a recipe. store_query values were verified to land in the intended CATEGORY, not just to match the word: 'muffins' returned ENGLISH muffins, 'biscuits' returned Belvita cookies, and 'donuts' returned Dunkin K-CUP COFFEE. The `why` text also avoids quoting an exact score, because the number shown on the card moves with the user's filters and diet profile and the copy would contradict it. `recipe` (added 2026-10-02) is our own short method for the listed ingredients - the full-screen recipe page (recipe.html?id=...) shows it; `pantry` lists salt/pepper-type items that are assumed on hand and are not added to the shopping list. Muffins gained 1/3 cup honey: without any sweetener the listed ingredients make bread rolls, not muffins.

items.title: Granola
items.effort: Stir, spread on a tray, 25 minutes in the oven
items.why: Store granola is where oats meet a surprising amount of sugar and oil. Yours is oats plus whatever you actually want in it.

recipe.intro: Crunchy clusters with no added oils you wouldn't cook with yourself, sweetened only with honey. Make a batch on Sunday and it lasts the week.
steps: Heat the oven to 325°F and line a rimmed baking sheet with parchment.
Roughly chop the almonds. In a large bowl, stir the oats, almonds, cinnamon and a pinch of salt together.
Warm the honey and olive oil together for 20 seconds in the microwave so they pour easily, then pour over the oats and stir until every oat is coated.
Spread it out in an even layer and press it down firmly with the back of a spatula - pressing is what makes clusters.
Bake 12 minutes, rotate the pan, and bake another 10-13 minutes until golden at the edges. Don't stir if you want big clusters.
Let it cool completely on the pan (it crisps as it cools), then break it into pieces.
tips: Add dried fruit only after baking - it burns in the oven.
Swap almonds for walnuts or pecans, or add 1/4 cup pumpkin seeds.
recipe.storage: Airtight jar at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.

items.title: Vinaigrette
items.why: Bottled dressing needs emulsifiers and preservatives to survive a shelf. A jar in your fridge does not.

recipe.intro: The classic 3-to-1 dressing. Store-bought versions are mostly soybean or canola oil; this is olive oil, vinegar and not much else.
steps: Finely grate or mince the garlic clove.
Put the vinegar, mustard, garlic, salt and a few grinds of pepper in a jar and shake for a few seconds.
Add the olive oil, close the lid and shake hard for 20-30 seconds until it turns creamy.
Taste on a leaf of lettuce and adjust - a little more salt, or a splash more vinegar if you like it sharper.
tips: The mustard is what holds it together - don't skip it.
A teaspoon of honey rounds it out if your vinegar is very sharp.
recipe.storage: Fridge for up to 1 week. The olive oil firms up when cold - let it sit out 10 minutes and shake again.

items.title: Salsa
items.effort: Chop, or pulse in a food processor. 10 minutes
items.why: Jarred salsa is cooked so it keeps. Fresh is a different food, and the ingredient list is four things.

recipe.intro: Restaurant-style salsa from a can of tomatoes, ready in ten minutes, with nothing in it you can't pronounce.
equipment: Food processor or blender (or a knife and cutting board)
steps: Drain the diced tomatoes in a colander for a couple of minutes so the salsa isn't watery.
Roughly chop the onion and the cilantro (leaves and tender stems).
Put the onion, cilantro, the juice of the lime and the salt in a food processor and pulse 3-4 times.
Add the tomatoes and pulse a few more times, just until it's as chunky or smooth as you like it.
Taste and adjust with more salt or lime. It's even better after 30 minutes in the fridge.
tips: For heat, add a seeded jalapeño with the onion.
No food processor? Finely chop everything and stir it together.

items.title: Hummus
items.why: Store hummus carries preservatives so it survives shipping. Yours is five things and tastes like chickpeas.

recipe.intro: Smoother and brighter than the tub, and made with olive oil instead of the soybean or canola oil many brands use.
steps: Drain the chickpeas and rinse them. Save a few to put on top if you like.
Put the tahini and the juice of the lemon in the food processor and blend 1 minute, until thick and pale.
Add the garlic, salt, 2 tbsp of the olive oil (and the cumin if using) and blend 30 seconds.
Add the chickpeas and blend 1-2 minutes, scraping down the sides.
With the machine running, add ice-cold water a tablespoon at a time until it turns smooth and fluffy - cold water is what makes it whipped instead of pasty.
Spoon into a bowl, swirl the top and drizzle with the last tablespoon of olive oil.
tips: Blending the tahini and lemon first is what makes it fluffy instead of pasty.
Very cold water makes it smoother.
recipe.storage: Fridge for up to 5 days, covered.

items.title: Pasta sauce
items.why: The good jars are genuinely good — this one is closer than most. Worth it for the ones that are not.

recipe.intro: A simple marinara: tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and onion. Most jars add sugar and seed oil; this needs neither.
recipe.servings: enough for 1 lb of pasta (4 servings)
pantry: Optional: a pinch of red pepper flakes, a few basil leaves
steps: Finely chop the onion and thinly slice the garlic.
Warm the olive oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and translucent.
Add the garlic (and pepper flakes if using) and cook 1 minute, until fragrant - don't let it brown.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and the rest of the salt. Bring to a gentle bubble, then turn the heat to low.
Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until slightly thickened.
Taste and adjust the salt. Tear in basil at the end if you have it.
tips: If the sauce tastes sharp, simmer a few minutes longer rather than adding sugar.
Toss the pasta in the sauce with a splash of pasta water so it clings.
recipe.storage: Fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.

items.title: Guacamole
items.why: Packaged guacamole is pressure-treated to stay green. Four ingredients and a fork gets you there.

recipe.intro: Store guacamole often relies on preservatives to stay green. Fresh takes five minutes and needs four things.
steps: Very finely chop the onion and the cilantro.
Halve the avocados, remove the pits and scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Add the juice of the lime and the salt, and mash with a fork - leave it a little chunky.
Stir in the onion and cilantro. Taste and add more salt or lime.
tips: Ripe avocados give slightly when pressed near the stem.
Press plastic wrap right onto the surface to stop it browning.
recipe.storage: Best the same day. Fridge up to 1 day with plastic pressed onto the surface.

items.title: Blueberry muffins
items.why: Packaged muffins are cake with a different name — the whole shelf scores in the teens, so there is no careful pick to make here. These take one bowl.

recipe.intro: Store muffins are some of the lowest-scoring things in the bakery aisle. These are sweetened with honey and made with butter, real milk and eggs.
steps: Heat the oven to 375°F and line a 12-cup muffin tin with paper liners.
Melt the butter and let it cool for a few minutes.
In a large bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder and salt.
In another bowl, whisk the eggs, milk, honey and melted butter until smooth.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and fold gently with a spatula until just combined - a few lumps are fine. Overmixing makes muffins tough.
Fold in the blueberries, then divide the batter between the 12 cups (about 3/4 full).
Bake 20-24 minutes, until golden and a toothpick in the center comes out clean.
Cool 5 minutes in the tin, then move to a rack.
tips: Frozen blueberries work - add them straight from frozen so they don't bleed.
Toss the berries in a spoonful of the flour so they don't sink.
recipe.storage: Room temperature 2 days, or freeze up to 3 months.

items.title: Buttermilk biscuits
items.effort: Cut butter into flour, 15 minutes in the oven
items.why: Tube biscuits are built around dough conditioners and hydrogenated fat so they survive refrigeration. Nothing in the aisle escapes it. Four ingredients does.

recipe.intro: Tall, flaky buttermilk biscuits with five ingredients - no shortening, no dough conditioners.
steps: Heat the oven to 425°F and line a baking sheet with parchment.
Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
Cut the cold butter into small cubes and work it into the flour with a pastry cutter or your fingertips until it looks like coarse crumbs with some pea-sized pieces.
Pour in the cold buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy dough forms.
Turn it onto a floured counter, pat into a rectangle about 1 inch thick, fold it in half, and pat out again. Repeat twice - this makes the layers.
Cut out biscuits straight down without twisting, and place them touching on the sheet.
Bake 12-15 minutes until tall and golden brown on top.
tips: Keep the butter and buttermilk cold until the moment you use them.
Pressing the cutter straight down (no twisting) is what lets them rise tall.
recipe.storage: Best warm. Room temperature 2 days; freeze unbaked biscuits and bake from frozen, adding 3-4 minutes.

items.title: Honey mustard dressing
items.why: Every bottled version is sweetened and stabilised to sit on a shelf. It is four things you already have, and it takes less time than reading the label.

recipe.intro: Bottled honey mustard is the dressing where nothing scores well. This one is four ingredients and two minutes.
equipment: Bowl and whisk, or a jar with a lid
steps: Put the mustard, honey, vinegar, salt and pepper in a bowl or jar.
Whisk (or shake) until smooth.
Slowly whisk in the olive oil until thick and glossy.
Taste - add more honey for sweeter, more vinegar for tangier.
tips: It doubles as a dip for chicken or a glaze for salmon.
Thin it with a teaspoon of water if it's too thick to drizzle.
